recipes.name: Old-School Baltimore Crab Soup
ingredients_raw: 2 tablespoons salt, or more to taste
2 tablespoons ground black pepper, or more to taste
1 pound green beans, cut into 1 inch pieces
2 tablespoons seafood seasoning (such as Old Bay®), or more to taste

steps.text: Bring a large pot of lightly salted water to a boil. Add carrots and cook until tender, about 5 minutes. Drain well and set aside.

Place ham bone, barley, salt, and pepper in large stockpot with 4 cups water. Simmer over medium heat for 30 to 45 minutes. Add cabbage and tomatoes and continue to simmer for 15 more minutes. Stir in potatoes and carrots; simmer until potatoes are tender and easily pierced with a fork, 20 to 30 minutes. Stir in 1 cup water, corn, green beans, lima beans, and peas; simmer for 20 minutes.

While the soup is simmering, clean crabs by opening them and discarding the lungs and mouth. Remove the yellowish-brown tomalley (fat) and set aside. Break crabs in half and add to the soup along with seafood seasoning. Simmer for 20 minutes, stirring occasionally.
Meanwhile, cook bacon in a large, deep skillet over medium-high heat, turning occasionally, until evenly browned, about 10 minutes. Drain on a paper towel-lined plate; reserve grease in the skillet.

Cook and stir reserved tomalley in bacon grease over low heat until mixture becomes gravy-like. Stir cooked tomalley into the soup with remaining 1 cup water. Continue simmering for 45 minutes, then add lump crabmeat and season with additional salt, pepper, and seafood seasoning if necessary. Simmer for 1 hour and 15 minutes, stirring occasionally. Reduce the heat to low until ready to serve.

raw_recipe.headline: Old-School Baltimore Crab Soup
raw_recipe.description: This traditional Baltimore crab soup is a staple at most Maryland cookouts. The long and slow simmering results in an extra-rich and tasty broth.

review.reviewBody: This was a great soup! Female crabs are called "sooks" and fallis a great time to buy them cheap. You want to include the "coral" red stuff that is inthe cavities as well as the mustard to really get the flavor. It looks weird, but don't throw it out! I added an onion and a stalk of celery to this, because I've never heard of crab soup without it. Other than that, I used half water and half homemade veggie stock and it was incredible! Thanks for the recipe!

As a Baltimore native (71 years), this is close to classic except we would never sully crab soup with barley or potatoes. The cabbage is key, and I started with a ham stock made from a huge shank bone (also classic in East Baltimore/Highlandtown). Fresh summer corn is what really makes it.

Being a Baltimore native, this isn’t the recipe I grew up eating at family crab feasts. We cooked steamed crab claws in water with beef broth & beer, lump crab , tomatoes, green beans & corn, diced potatoes, ground pepper & Old Bay. No barley or other veggies, though chopped cabbage was nice.
I have lived in Baltimore MD my whole life 40+ yrs. This is the real deal

I made a few changes this was the first time I made crab soup so I left out barley,ham and added 2 lb of crab and 6 crabs,and lots of old bay,and used a soup bone that I cooked for and hour and a half and one beef cube with lot of water.
Amazing! Skipped barley and potato. I'm from MD and this is the best. That is all.

I am not from this area and have never tried this soup but I loved it and I am now a big fan! I added chunked ham from the bone instead of bacon and used local (NC) crab and It was amazing. my picky children loved it too!

I made this soup as best I could. Whole blue crabs were not available, so I ended up having to use all pre-packaged blue crab meat (I used a full pound.). I'm sure my soup wasn't as flavorful, but it was still good. The lack of whole crabs also meant that I did not have any tomalleys to work with. I also didn't pre-cook the carrots; I just added cut up carrots to the soup when I added the tomatoes and cabbage. The soup simmers long enough to cook the carrots. I also used fresh green beans, so I added those in the same time I added the potatoes to be sure that they had enough time to cook. I note that the recipe never says when to remove the ham bone or whether to cut off the remaining ham and put it back into the soup. I did. After about two-three hours of simmering, I removed the bone and returned bite-sized pieces of ham to the soup. The recipe also never says whether to put the cooked bacon in the soup. I assume you crumble the bacon and add it in towards the end. Since I didn't have any tomalleys, I skipped the bacon step altogether. As for seasoning, I used 2 T each of salt, black pepper, and Old Bay, as instructed. I thought the finished soup had a bit of a spicy bite to it, so I may cut back on the pepper next time. Even without the whole crab, tomalleys and bacon, it was still good. I will try making this again when I can get whole blue crabs.

I'm from Baltimore and this recipe is the real deal. It's excellent! I added onion and celery because that's the way my mother made it. I prefer it w/o the barley, but that's just me. My mother said that if there was a thunderstorm while the soup was cooking that it would be ruined. I don't know about that part, but I've always kept it in mind! I like to add some local crab meat too.
Lifelong Marylander here and this soup was just perfect! Tastes like real crab soup and not just some tomato based veggie soup with some Old Bay thrown in . Thanks for the recipe. Keeper for sure!
Old school crab soup is the real thing. I have made it for years this way. The best and served in restaurants every where even OC.
